nameStory: This fungus gets its spooky name from its dark, mysterious appearance that seems to bubble up from dead wood like something from a witch's cauldron. The 'butter' part comes from its soft, gelatinous texture that feels surprisingly smooth and slippery when touched. European folklore associated these dark, blob-like fungi with witchcraft and magic potions.
description: Black Witches' Butter is a distinctive jelly fungus that looks like shiny, dark blobs or blisters growing on dead wood. These gelatinous masses are typically black or very dark brown, with a glossy, wet appearance even when dry. Individual fruit bodies can grow up to about an inch wide, often clustering together in groups. Unlike typical mushrooms with caps and stems, this fungus forms irregularly shaped, bumpy masses that feel like firm jelly.

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Distinctly gelatinous and rubbery, feeling like firm jelly or thick gelatin when fresh; bounces back when poked gently

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Shiny black to very dark brown, with a glossy, wet-looking surface that reflects light

idTips.label: Shape
idTips.description: Irregular, blister-like or brain-shaped masses without distinct caps or stems; often bumpy or warty in appearance

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual masses up to about 1.2 inches wide, but often grow in clusters that can span several inches

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Always grows on dead wood, particularly favoring oak branches that are still attached to trees

idTips.label: Safety Note
idTips.description: Never eat any wild mushroom or fungus without expert identification - while not known to be highly toxic, proper identification requires expertise

habitat: Look for Black Witches' Butter on dead branches of deciduous trees, especially oak, throughout New England's forests and woodlands. It particularly favors dead branches that are still attached to living trees rather than fallen logs. You'll find it in both mixed hardwood forests and oak-dominated areas from sea level to moderate elevations.

seasonality.spring: Fresh fruit bodies begin appearing as temperatures warm and spring rains provide moisture. Look for small, newly formed black blobs on dead oak branches.
seasonality.summer: Peak fruiting season with abundant, plump specimens after summer rainstorms. The gelatinous masses are at their largest and most noticeable during humid periods.
seasonality.fall: Continues fruiting through autumn rains, often persisting on branches as temperatures drop. Older specimens may become darker and more wrinkled.
seasonality.winter: Fruit bodies can persist through winter, becoming dried and shrunken but rehydrating with moisture. Less noticeable but still present on dead branches.

funFact: This remarkable fungus can completely dry out to a hard, shriveled black crust during drought, then magically plump back up to its full jelly-like form within hours of the next rainstorm - essentially bringing itself back from the dead!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with Warlock's Butter (Exidia nigricans), but Black Witches' Butter has a distinctly warty, blistered surface while Warlock's Butter is smoother. Remember: 'Witches are warty, Warlocks are smooth.'
contextualKnowledge: Despite the dramatic name, there's actually a whole family of 'butter' fungi with different colors - you might also find Yellow Witches' Butter and Orange Jelly fungus in New England. The 'witches' butter' name is sometimes applied to different species in different regions, so the scientific name is your best bet for accurate identification.
compareHints: Black Witches' Butter stands out from its Exidia relatives by its distinctly warty, blister-like surface texture and preference for oak wood. American Amber Jelly Fungus is similar in texture but amber-colored rather than black, while other jelly fungi in the area tend to be smoother or differently colored. The bumpy, brain-like surface combined with the deep black color makes this species fairly distinctive among New England's jelly fungi.

relatedSpecies.distinction: American Amber Jelly differs from its close relative Black Witches' Butter by staying consistently amber to orange-brown rather than turning black with age.

Amber jelly differs from its relatives mainly by substrate preference - while Black Witches' Butter grows on various hardwoods and appears darker, and birch jelly sticks to birch trees, amber jelly is the willow specialist.
